lessons.title: Urbanization, Migration and the Changing Shape of India's Labour Force

children.text: The last lesson ended with a preview: workers from Bihar and Uttar Pradesh filling jobs in an aging Kerala and Tamil Nadu. That single example sits inside a much larger, still-unfolding story, India's transition from a mostly rural country to a majority urban one, and the internal migration that transition is built on. This lesson works through both, and why they matter directly to how productively India's working-age window gets used.
India's Urbanization Rate: Still Surprisingly Low

For an economy of India's size and global visibility, its urbanization rate is still comparatively low. Roughly a third of Indians live in urban areas today, against close to two-thirds in China and well over three-quarters in most developed economies. This is not a sign India is behind on some universal schedule, it reflects a genuinely different, more gradual urban transition, but it does mean a large share of the productivity gains that typically come with urbanization are still ahead of India rather than behind it.

body.text: The 1991, 2001, and 2011 figures are Census of India data and are reasonably solid. The 2023 estimate and the 2036 and 2050 projections are rounded and illustrative, since India's last full Census was due in 2021 and has been delayed, and long-run urban projections vary by source. Verify current figures from the Census of India or UN World Urbanization Prospects before citing them elsewhere.

children.text: India's internal migration is large enough that measuring it properly required an unusual approach. The Economic Survey of 2016-17 used unreserved railway ticket sales as a proxy, since most low-income interstate labour migrants travel this way, and estimated roughly 9 million people migrating across state lines for work each year through the first half of the 2010s, implying a cumulative interstate migrant workforce of around 60 million. Bihar and Uttar Pradesh were, and remain, the two largest source states, sending workers primarily toward Delhi-NCR, Maharashtra, Gujarat, and Punjab, alongside the southern corridor covered in the last lesson.

children.text: COVID-19's Migrant Crisis: A Stress Test

The scale and fragility of this migrant workforce became visible to the entire country in a matter of weeks in March 2020. The sudden nationwide lockdown left millions of migrant workers without income, housing security, or a way home, triggering one of the largest internal population movements India has seen in peacetime. Government data show several million migrant workers were transported home on special 'Shramik' trains alone in the months that followed, on top of many more who travelled by road, often on foot, over hundreds of kilometres.

body.text: The 2020 migrant crisis exposed structural gaps that had existed for decades but rarely made headlines: most interstate migrants worked informally, without portable social security benefits, formal housing, or registration in their destination state, leaving them acutely exposed the moment normal economic activity stopped. This is directly relevant to how resilient India's urban labour supply actually is, not just how large it is.

children.text: Where the Jobs Actually Are: Agriculture's Shrinking, Outsized Share

body.caption: Employment Share vs GDP Share, Illustrative

body.text: This table is the productivity story behind urbanization, in numbers. Agriculture employs roughly two and a half times its share of GDP, meaning output per worker there is far below the national average, while services produce nearly double their employment share, at much higher output per worker. Every worker who moves from low-productivity farm labour into even a modest urban services or industry job raises India's average output per worker, mechanically, without requiring any new technology or investment. This is a large part of why urbanization is treated as a growth lever in its own right, not just a side effect of growth.

children.text: This is the strain side of urbanization: infrastructure, housing, and services in destination cities have often struggled to keep pace with the speed of inward migration. The government's response has centred on three major programmes launched in 2015, the Smart Cities Mission targeting 100 cities, AMRUT (Atal Mission for Rejuvenation and Urban Transformation) focused on basic infrastructure, and PM Awas Yojana-Urban targeting affordable housing, all aimed at closing this gap between how fast people are arriving and how fast cities can actually absorb them.

body.title: Reading a Migration-Driven Growth Story
body.scenario: A state government proudly announces that its urban population grew 25% over the past decade, and a news report frames this purely as a sign of the state's economic success.
body.prompt: Based on this lesson, what two follow-up questions would you want answered before accepting that framing?
body.modelAnswer: First, is this growth coming primarily from natural urban population increase and local rural-to-urban shifts, or largely from interstate in-migration, since the latter says more about opportunity relative to other states than about this state's own economic transformation specifically. Second, has the state's urban infrastructure, housing, and formal job creation kept pace with that population growth, or is a rising share of new urban residents landing in slum-type or informal conditions, as roughly 17% of urban India did per the last available Census. Rapid urban population growth without matching formal job creation and infrastructure is not automatically a success story, it can just as easily signal strain.

body.title: Quick Check: Why Urbanization Raises Productivity
body.question: Based on the employment-versus-GDP table in this lesson, why does a worker moving from agriculture to a services job in a city tend to raise national output per worker, even without any change in technology?
options: Because urban jobs always pay in foreign currency
Because agriculture employs a much larger share of workers than its share of GDP, while services do the reverse, so shifting a worker from one to the other raises average output per worker
Because agricultural workers are less educated than services workers
There is no productivity effect, this is a common misconception
body.explanation: Agriculture employs roughly two and a half times its share of GDP in this lesson's illustrative figures, meaning output per worker there is well below the national average, while services generate nearly double their employment share of GDP, meaning output per worker there is well above average. Moving a worker from the first group to the second mechanically raises average output per worker, which is exactly why urbanization is treated as a genuine productivity lever, not just a demographic side effect.

body.text: India's urbanization is not just people moving to cities. It is the single largest available lever for converting a still-underemployed rural workforce into the higher-productivity jobs that actually determine whether the working-age window from the last two lessons turns into growth or into strain.

points: India remains comparatively under-urbanized, at roughly 36% urban today against China's roughly 65%, meaning much of the productivity gain typically associated with urbanization is still ahead of India rather than behind it.

The Economic Survey 2016-17 estimated India's cumulative interstate migrant workforce at roughly 60 million, based on railway ticketing data, with Bihar and Uttar Pradesh as the largest source states.

The 2020 COVID-19 lockdown exposed how informally most interstate migrants work, without portable benefits or housing security, a structural vulnerability separate from the sheer scale of the migration itself.

Agriculture employs roughly two and a half times its share of India's GDP, while services generate nearly double their employment share, which is why shifting workers from agriculture to urban services or industry mechanically raises national productivity.

Major migration corridors, Bihar and UP toward Delhi-NCR and Maharashtra, Odisha and Jharkhand toward western and southern industrial hubs, are already reshaping India's urban labour force, straining infrastructure even as government programmes like Smart Cities, AMRUT, and PMAY-Urban try to keep pace.
